title: Drugging the Undruggable: New Ways to Repair or Destroy Cancer’s Toughest Targets

summary: Background: In health systems, AI is increasingly being implemented as a form of clinical decision support (CDS). Research on patient perspectives, however, lags behind clinician-focused studies. Before the introduction of AI-based tools, clinicians often used and continue to use rule-based guidelines and risk calculators (RCs) to inform decision-making. Prior research has shown that RCs for CDS have mixed effects on patient adherence to treatment recommendations, whereas for AI-based tools, the effect is still not clear. Objective: This study aims to assess differences in patients’ behavioral intentions, trust, and preferences for clinical recommendations provided by doctors alone, doctors supported by RCs, and doctors supported by AI-based risk predictions. We also evaluate how sociodemographic characteristics affect these perceptions. Methods: We surveyed 1185 US-based adults. Participants rated their likelihood of taking recommended clinical actions (behavioral intentions) across 6 clinical scenarios, where they were randomized to a different recommendation source (doctor, doctor + RC, and doctor + AI). Participants also rated their trust in the recommendation, indicated their preferred source for recommendations, and provided qualitative feedback. Results: Behavioral intentions differed by recommendation source such that the doctor + RC condition had greater odds of behavioral intention than the doctor + AI condition. Behavioral intentions were also affected by the clinical condition. Participants had greater odds of trusting doctors alone over doctor + RC, and both doctors alone and doctor + RC had greater trust than doctor + AI. However, a plurality of participants ultimately preferred a doctor using an RC for making recommendations. Several sociodemographic differences were detected, namely, participants with higher subjective numeracy and literacy had higher odds of taking clinical action and higher trust across decision-support sources. We detected qualitative themes in the following categories: decision quality and reliability; trust and perceptions; patient-centeredness and autonomy; fairness, transparency, and ethics. Across categories, participants reported skepticism toward all decision sources and potential misunderstanding of AI’s ability to personalize risk predictions. Some participants also stated that they had no additional concerns or were uncertain regarding their feelings. Conclusions: These findings reveal novel, nuanced patient preferences shaped by task and context, offering guidance for aligning AI-supported care with patient values. Patients were not aligned on the recommendation source across intentions, trust, and preferences. Taken together, our results indicate that patients prefer doctors working with easy-to-understand, explainable support but are still learning to trust these tools. Our findings also highlight the continued importance of the clinical context and its interaction with computer-assisted decision support. Future work should evaluate how we can transparently convey to patients the use of AI in clinical decision-making, embedded within the given clinical context. This may present an opportunity to bolster, rather than erode, patient trust.
title: Investigating Patient Trust and Intention to Act in AI-Supported Clinical Decisions: Cross-Sectional Survey

summary: Clinical AI governance has advanced rapidly in technical validation, regulatory compliance, risk management, human oversight, and postdeployment monitoring. Yet a more fundamental question often remains implicit: under what conditions are health institutions justified in exercising consequential authority through AI over patients, clinicians, and communities? In this Viewpoint, we argue that legitimacy should be recognized as an independent governance requirement, distinct from technical assurance, legal and ethical compliance, trust, acceptance, and institutional approval. Our aim is to distinguish institutional approval from public authorization and to propose a normative framework for authorizing consequential clinical AI deployments. We address health system leaders, clinical AI governance and procurement teams, frontline clinicians, and patient and community representatives. Drawing on theories of legitimacy and public value and published clinical AI governance research, we make the following contributions: (1) the concept of the unclaimed decision, defined as a consequential choice about purpose, threshold, population, or priority for which no actor clearly assumes responsibility for public justification; (2) a tripartite framework comprising procedural authorization, substantive justification, and relational renewal; and (3) practical governance tools to support public justification, contestation, and renewal. These tools include 3 minimum auditable conditions: visibility of deployment; affected-party input before governing conditions are fixed; and conditional reviewability, which requires a predefined trigger that can be invoked by a named actor outside the deploying team. A 5-question public authorization test examines purpose, distribution, exclusion, meaningful choice and contestability, and renewal. Governance intensity should increase with clinical consequence; distributive reach; difficulty of reversal; and the absence of genuine, informed choice. For smaller health care organizations, we propose ways to perform the same core governance functions through existing advisory bodies, targeted interviews, shared regional resources, and standardized documentation. We also outline a heuristic for identifying affected publics, procedures for specifying participation authority and resolving disagreement, and procurement provisions that preserve reviewability across vendor boundaries. These are normative proposals requiring evaluation. Public authorization requires continuing substantive justification; it cannot be inferred from compliance, popularity, or completion of an audit checklist.
title: Institutional Approval Is Not Public Authorization: Legitimacy as a Governance Requirement for Clinical AI

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Female university students encounter appearance ideals, comparison cues, and appearance-related pressure across traditional and digital media environments. These sociocultural influences may coexist with psychological resources such as body appreciation and weight-control self-efficacy. However, variable-centered analyses may obscure heterogeneity in how these characteristics are combined within individuals. The measures used in this study assessed broader sociocultural appearance-related attitudes rather than platform-specific digital exposure. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to identify latent profiles characterized by ideal-body internalization, appearance comparison, perceived media pressure, body appreciation, and weight-control self-efficacy among female university students and to examine whether these profiles differed in moderate-intensity exercise duration, self-perceived body size, and screen-based sedentary behavior. <strong>Methods:</strong> A cross-sectional online survey was conducted between May and June 2025 among 2034 female students recruited by convenience sampling from 1 comprehensive university in China. Latent profile analysis compared 1- through 6-profile solutions. Model selection considered information criteria, likelihood-ratio tests, entropy, profile size, parsimony, and substantive interpretability. Distal outcomes were compared using the Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars (BCH) procedure for continuous outcomes and the distal categorical outcome (DCAT) procedure for categorical outcomes. Sensitivity analyses examined alternative exercise definitions, transformations, extreme-value handling, sociodemographic adjustment, and self-reported BMI. Conventionally calculated weekly moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) outcomes were examined among 1056 participants with complete activity data. The primary analysis preserved classification uncertainty, and supplementary models assessed the robustness of associations without treating most-likely profile membership as error-free. No population-prevalence inference was intended. <strong>Results:</strong> A 4-profile solution was retained (entropy=0.874): very low sociocultural attitudes—higher body appreciation (137/2034, 6.74%), average sociocultural attitudes (1081/2034, 53.15%), lower sociocultural attitudes (452/2034, 22.22%), and higher sociocultural attitudes (364/2034, 17.9%). Solutions with 5 and 6 profiles each contained a very small class of approximately 1.7% (35/2034), and the adjusted Lo-Mendell-Rubin test comparing 6 vs 5 profiles was nonsignificant (<i>P</i>=.47). The profiles were differentiated primarily by a low-to-high gradient in appearance comparison, ideal-body internalization, and perceived media pressure. Moderate-intensity exercise duration differed across profiles in the primary analysis (BCH Wald <i>χ</i><sup>2</sup><sub>3</sub>=15.3; <i>P</i>=.002), but complete-case weekly MVPA did not (<i>P</i>=.52). Body-size perception differed in the unadjusted analysis (DCAT <i>χ</i><sup>2</sup><sub>9</sub>=20.4; <i>P</i>=.02), although the overall association was not independent of sociodemographic characteristics and self-reported BMI. Weekly screen-use categories did not differ significantly across profiles (DCAT <i>χ</i><sup>2</sup><sub>12</sub>=16.7; <i>P</i>=.16). <strong>Conclusions:</strong> The retained profiles were sample-specific statistical configurations that largely represented a sociocultural low-to-high gradient rather than 4 clearly discrete psychological types. Associations with exercise and body-size perception were modest and sensitive to outcome definition or covariate adjustment. The cross-sectional findings do not establish causal direction or digital media mechanisms. Longitudinal, multisite studies incorporating direct measures of digital exposure, exercise motivation, objectively assessed activity, and measured anthropometry are needed.
title: Sociocultural Appearance-Related Attitudes and Psychological Resources and Their Associations With Moderate-Intensity Exercise, Body Size Perception, and Screen Time Among Female University Students: Cross-Sectional Latent Profile Analysis

summary: Background: Bipolar disorder (BP) affects 1% to 3% of adults worldwide, with diagnostic delays averaging 6 years and high initial misdiagnosis rates. The absence of objective diagnostic measures contributes to clinical uncertainty and suboptimal outcomes. Objective: This study aimed to (1) develop a machine learning model for BP diagnosis and mood state classification using linguistic and acoustic features, (2) identify features associated with different mood states by comparing each with healthy controls (HC), and (3) explore whether features distinguish between mood states within BP. Methods: We analyzed data prospectively collected over 7 years from 61 patients with BP and 99 HC across Japan. Speech samples were collected via semistructured interviews over 1 to 5 visits and analyzed cross-sectionally, using aggregated or single-visit observations per participant rather than within-person longitudinal modeling. We extracted 6373 acoustic features (openSMILE 3.0, ComParE 2016) and 211 linguistic features. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)–regularized logistic regression with nested cross-validation and age- and sex-matched undersampling was used. Mood states were classified as depressive state (DS; Hamilton Depression Rating Scale-17 [HAMD-17] ≥8, Young Mania Rating Scale [YMRS] ≤7), state with manic/mixed symptoms (MS/MX; YMRS ≥8), or euthymic state (ES; HAMD-17 ≤7, YMRS ≤7). Seven classification tasks included BP vs HC, each mood state vs HC, and interstate comparisons. Feature importance was validated via permutation testing (<.05). Medication sensitivity analyses were performed. Results: The model achieved high discrimination for BP vs HC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]=0.916, 95% CI 0.854‐0.958; sensitivity 0.933; specificity 0.859) and strong performance for mood states vs HC (AUC=0.805‐0.874). Acoustic features comprised 96% to 98% of the features achieving statistical significance (<.05), including mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, spectral characteristics, and voice quality measures, showing strong correlations with diagnostic probabilities (|ρ|=0.35‐0.85) and symptom severity (HAMD-17: ρ=–0.51; YMRS: ρ=–0.37); 2 to 4 linguistic features per comparison also reached significance. With sample independence ensured for interstate comparisons, DS vs ES significantly exceeded chance (AUC=0.760, permutation =.03), whereas MS/MX vs ES (AUC=0.601, =.20) and DS vs MS/MX (AUC=0.569, =.30) did not, suggesting that markers primarily reflect persistent disease characteristics with partial state-associated components in depressive states. Conclusions: The combined acoustic-linguistic model, driven primarily by acoustic features, shows potential as an objective aid for BP diagnosis (AUC>0.9), largely free of medication confounding; some features remained detectable during euthymia, although ES discrimination could not be fully separated from concurrent antipsychotic treatment. Although DS showed partial distinguishability from ES, overall limitations remain for monitoring mood state changes. Findings require validation in diverse populations and against other psychiatric conditions.
title: Machine Learning Classification of Bipolar Disorder Across Mood States Using Natural Language Processing and Speech Analysis: Observational Study

summary: Background: Limited data availability and privacy constraints hinder the development of robust survival prediction models for personalized treatment. Synthetic data offers a promising solution, preserving the statistical properties of real clinical data. Objective: This study aimed to quantitatively assess the feasibility of using synthetic data for survival prediction by evaluating model transfer performance to real-world hospital data, with a focus on model transfer strategies. Methods: We developed and validated colorectal cancer survival prediction models using the National Cancer Data Center (NCDC) synthetic data (30,683 patients from 3 Korean institutions) for pretraining and real hospital data (2170 patients from Hwasun Jeonnam University Hospital) for external validation. We evaluated 3 model transfer strategies—domain adaptation, zero-shot, and ensemble—using extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) and light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM). In total, 48 model configurations were tested, defined by the combination of algorithms (LightGBM and XGBoost), sampling technique (no-sampling, random undersampling [RUS], and synthetic minority oversampling technique combined with edited nearest neighbors [SMOTEENN]), model type (baseline, domain adaptation, zero-shot, and ensemble), and optimization objective (area under the precision-recall curve [AUPRC] and ). The outcome was 7-year overall survival, evaluated using the AUPRC and Brier scores. Performance was compared against a hospital-only baseline using absolute values and deltas (ΔAUPRC and ΔBrier). Differences and corresponding 95% CIs were estimated on the held-out test set using 2000 bootstrap samples. Results: Zero-shot application reduced the AUPRC in most settings, and any marginal improvements observed in the remaining settings were not statistically significant. In contrast, the domain adaptation model improved AUPRC in 8/12 combinations, with 4 statistically significant gains; the best setting (XGBoost+RUS+ optimization) achieved AUPRC=0.5391 (Δ+0.1474; <.001). The soft ensemble increased AUPRC in 7/12 combinations, with 3 statistically significant gains; the best setting (XGBoost+RUS+AUPRC optimization) achieved AUPRC=0.5060 (+0.1258, =.002). For calibration, Brier scores improved in most domain adaptation and ensemble combinations, with a substantial proportion reaching statistical significance. Conclusions: When domain adaptation using local hospital data was applied, the model pretrained on synthetic data exhibited similar performance to the hospital-only baseline across various settings. This study demonstrates the methodological utility of a model transfer approach using NCDC synthetic data in a setting with limited data sharing. At the same time, it clarifies that while synthetic data can serve as a complement to local clinical data, it is not a substitute for real-world clinical models.
title: Correction: Evaluation of the Applicability of Synthetic Data in the Development of Colorectal Cancer Survival Prediction Models: External Validation of Advanced Machine Learning Models Based on National Cancer Data Center Data

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> The human-horse bond has played a role in human development throughout history and has more recently been applied to mental health promotion through equine-assisted learning (EAL) programs. In EAL settings, therapeutic documentation and assessment commonly rely on practitioner observations documented through behavioral checklists, structured interviews, and progress notes, which can pose challenges due to time demands, subjectivity, and inconsistent standardization across practitioners and contexts. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to address these challenges in the context of mental health promotion programs. This study developed an AI-powered digital health framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to analyze child-horse therapeutic interactions in EAL settings. The framework was developed in collaboration with the Yawardani Jan-ga EAL program, which supports the social and emotional well-being of Aboriginal youth in the Kimberley region of Western Australia. <strong>Methods:</strong> The proposed framework comprises three core components: (1) an activity classification module using a VLM with few-shot learning based on Sigmoid Loss for Language-Image Pre-training 2 (SigLIP2) to identify 9 therapeutic activities; (2) a proxemics analysis module using a Qwen2.5-VL-7B VLM to classify physical contact between the child and horse; and (3) a body posture analysis module applying multimodal chain-of-thought prompting and self-consistency techniques to classify children’s body posture into confidence-related states with interpretable reasoning. <strong>Results:</strong> The framework was developed and evaluated using real-world images collected during therapeutic sessions with Aboriginal children participating in the Yawardani Jan-ga program. The activity classification module achieved an accuracy of 90.6%, with macroaveraged precision, recall, and <i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-scores of 92.0%, 91.1%, and 91.1%, respectively, under the selected 2-shot configuration. The proxemics analysis module achieved an accuracy of 88.6%, with macroaveraged precision, recall, and <i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-scores of 89.0%, 88.0%, and 88.5%, respectively, under the 1-shot configuration. For the body posture analysis module, system reliability was assessed using internal consistency metrics, achieving an average consistency of 0.916, an agreement rate of 0.705, a rationale coherence of 0.857, and a vote entropy of 0.174. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Overall, the findings suggest that AI- and VLM-based approaches can provide complementary support for practitioner-led documentation and assessment of observable child-horse therapeutic interactions in EAL settings. These approaches may help reduce practitioner burden and strengthen the assessment of programs that promote children’s social and emotional well-being.
title: Multimodal Analysis of Child-Horse Therapeutic Interactions Using Vision-Language Models in an Australian Aboriginal Equine-Assisted Learning Program for Social and Emotional Well-Being: Development and Evaluation Study

summary: Background: Parkinson disease (PD) impairs mobility and motor function, making accurate mobility assessment important for effective management and treatment planning. Traditional clinical assessments often rely on periodic clinical evaluations, which may not capture day-to-day symptom fluctuations. Wearable devices offer a promising alternative with continuous, objective tracking of mobility (eg, gait). However, although these tools provide valuable insights for patients and clinicians, their successful implementation depends on their acceptability to users. Objective: This study aimed to explore the acceptability of wearable devices for remote continuous mobility monitoring in PD from the perspectives of people with PD and informal carers. Methods: This international qualitative study used purposive sampling to recruit a diverse sample of 72 people with PD and 20 informal carers from the United Kingdom, Ireland, Belgium, Germany, Spain, and the United States. Participants were recruited between June 2023 and February 2026 through multiple community-based routes. One-to-one semistructured interviews, conducted online, via telephone, or in person, explored views on wearable devices for digital mobility assessment. Interview data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s 6-phase reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Most people with PD were generally open to wearable monitoring when it could capture motor fluctuations between “on” and “off” periods that were difficult to convey during clinical appointments, reduce reliance on memory, provide objective evidence to support treatment and medication discussions and self-advocacy, and track changes in mobility over time, which some felt could be reassuring. Acceptability depended on devices having a clear purpose, requiring minimal effort, and being easy to use. Tremor, reduced dexterity, and “off” periods could make fastening straps, navigating menus, and charging devices difficult. Carers valued wearable monitoring for the reassurance and safety it offered, particularly fall detection, and for support with both clinical and everyday decision-making but emphasized that devices must operate passively and integrate into daily caregiving without adding burden. Conclusions: Wearable mobility monitoring was generally acceptable to people with PD and carers when it offered clear clinical value, fit easily into everyday life, and provided reassurance that remote monitoring would complement rather than replace clinical care. As PD mobility was experienced as a shared concern within the care relationship, the value of monitoring depended on how well it supported the wider care dyad rather than the person with PD alone. These findings suggest that successful implementation will require co-design with people with PD and carers, alongside thoughtful clinical integration, to ensure that wearable technologies are both acceptable and effective in practice.
title: Acceptability of Wearable Digital Devices for Remote Continuous Mobility Monitoring in People With Parkinson Disease and Carers: Qualitative Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Parental involvement in obesity interventions is considered essential for sustainable behavior change in children and adolescents with overweight or obesity; yet, the effectiveness of parent-involved digital health interventions (DHIs) and the influence of different delivery modalities remain unclear. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to synthesize the effects of parent-involved DHIs on adiposity-related outcomes and behaviors and explore potential moderators. <strong>Methods:</strong> Nine databases were searched from inception to December 2025 to identify eligible randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Primary outcomes were adiposity-related outcomes such as BMI; secondary outcomes were adiposity-related behaviors, including dietary behavior, physical activity, and sedentary behavior. Standardized mean differences (SMDs; Hedges <i>g</i>) on primary outcomes were pooled using random-effects models. Prespecified subgroup analyses examined DHI delivery modalities and parent-involved strategies. Secondary outcomes were synthesized narratively. Risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2), and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation). <strong>Results:</strong> Twenty-nine RCTs (4156 participants) were included, of which 22 contributed to the meta-analysis. Parent-involved DHIs produced a small but statistically significant reduction in BMI-related outcomes compared with controls (SMD=<i>−</i>0.11, 95% CI <i>−</i>0.19 to <i>−</i>0.04; <i>P</i>=.004; <i>I</i>²=0%). When stratified by control type, the pooled effect remained significant in trials using inactive controls (SMD=<i>−</i>0.15, 95% CI <i>−</i>0.25 to <i>−</i>0.04; <i>P</i>=.006; <i>I</i>²<i>=</i>0%), but not in trials using active controls (SMD=<i>−</i>0.07, 95% CI <i>−</i>0.19 to 0.04; <i>P</i>=.20; <i>I</i>²<i>=</i>0%). Subgroup differences on DHI delivery modalities and parent-involved strategies were not statistically significant. For adiposity-related behaviors, significant improvements were reported in 5 of 16 trials for dietary behaviors, 2 of 17 for physical activity, and 2 of 12 for sedentary behavior. The risk of bias was generally low to some concerns, and the overall certainty of evidence for BMI-related outcomes was moderate. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that parent-involved DHIs may produce a small improvement in BMI-related outcomes among children and adolescents with overweight or obesity. However, evidence for improvements in adiposity-related behaviors remains limited, and neither the optimal digital delivery modality nor the most effective parent-involved strategy has been established. Future research should refine these interventions to identify optimal strategies and confirm their effectiveness. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> PROSPERO CRD420251239829; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251239829
title: Effects of Parent-Involved Digital Health Interventions on Adiposity-Related Outcomes and Behaviors in Children and Adolescents With Overweight or Obesity: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for text-based emotional support. However, general-purpose LLMs may not consistently recognize emotional cues, adapt supportive strategies to contexts, or generate responses aligned with psychologically informed communication. The limited availability of large-scale, structured Chinese counseling data further constrains the development of models for context-sensitive emotional support. Objective: We developed and evaluated YuanChat, a family of specialized LLMs for context-sensitive emotional support; assessed whether E-URIAL improved response quality; and compared YuanChat with base LLMs. Methods: We constructed 2 datasets from anonymized real-world counseling sessions: ECD-3 (104,897 counselor response turns) for fine-tuning and (9413 manually annotated counselor responses). Annotations covered emotional support conversation stages (exploration, comfort, and action), counseling techniques (clarification, support, and challenge), and empathic effects. We developed 2 YuanChat variants using GLM-4-9B-Chat and Huozi 3.5 as backbone models using parameter-efficient fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We then developed E-URIAL, an inference-time framework combining predicted emotion and support strategy labels with retrieved labeled exemplars. Given the dialogue history through the help seeker’s latest utterance, each model generated a counselor-style response. We compared YuanChat with GPT-4, ERNIE 4.0, CharacterGLM, GLM-4-9B-Chat, and Huozi 3.5. The evaluation comprised (1) automatic evaluation on in-domain and external datasets, assessing empathy identification and empathic expression; (2) evaluation of empathy-related situational reasoning using an expert-developed multiple-choice benchmark; (3) evaluation by clinical experts (n=8) of empathic attunement, support strategy appropriateness, perceived helpfulness, and safety and professional boundary adherence; and (4) a complementary evaluation by volunteer master’s students in clinical and counseling psychology (n=50) of response fluency, empathy, and perceived helpfulness. Results: Fine-tuning increased YuanChat-Huozi3.5’s empathic expression score from 0.57 to 0.68; empathy identification score increased from 0.54 to 0.59. In expert evaluation, YuanChat-Huozi3.5 received a higher empathic attunement score than the base Huozi3.5 model (1.279 vs 0.327; mean difference 0.952, 95% CI 0.746‐1.152). Using professional counselor responses as the reference, the mean differences for YuanChat-Huozi3.5 were 0.148, 0.079, 0.039, and 0.002 in empathic attunement, supportive appropriateness, perceived helpfulness, and safety and professional boundary adherence, respectively. No statistically significant differences were detected between YuanChat-Huozi3.5 and the counselor references (all Holm-adjusted ≥.29). Higher scores were observed when E-URIAL was applied. When E-URIAL was applied with 3 retrieved exemplars, YuanChat-Huozi3.5 achieved an empathy identification score of 0.69 versus 0.59 without E-URIAL, an empathic expression score of 0.79 versus 0.68, and a perceived helpfulness score of 0.74 versus 0.61. Conclusions: The findings indicate that fine-tuning on real-world counseling data and annotating models with structured emotional support labels improved context-sensitive empathic responding in LLMs. Without updating model parameters, E-URIAL further improved empathy identification and empathic expression across multiple models. Together, these methods provide a scalable, theory-informed approach to enhancing the emotional support capabilities of LLMs.
title: A Multistage Fine-Tuning and Empathy Alignment Approach for an Emotional Support Dialogue System: Development and Evaluation Study
